lesson.title: Taking Control: Explicit Type Casting
lesson.summary: Explicit type casting uses functions like int(), float(), str(), and bool() to convert a value's type on purpose, most commonly when handling text input that needs to become a number.
lesson.body:
Explicit type casting is when a programmer directly calls a conversion function to change a value's type on purpose, rather than relying on Python to do it automatically, as it does with implicit conversion. Python provides built-in functions named after each core type for exactly this job: int(), float(), str(), and bool(). Each one takes a value and returns a new value of the requested type, without modifying the original object at all, which fits the same read-and-return pattern that string methods followed in the string type lesson.

The most common use case for explicit casting is handling text input, since data read from a user, a file, or a web request typically arrives as a string even when it represents a number. Consider this trace:

user_input = "25"
doubled = int(user_input) * 2
print(doubled)

Without the explicit int() call, user_input * 2 would instead compute "25" * 2, which is legal Python but does something completely different: it produces the string "2525" by repeating the text, not the number 50 you probably wanted. Casting user_input to an int first makes the multiplication numeric, and the trace correctly prints 50. This is a genuinely common bug in beginner code: forgetting to cast text input before doing arithmetic on it, and getting a repeated string instead of an error, which makes the mistake easy to miss.

Casting can also fail loudly, which is a feature, not a flaw. int("hello") raises a ValueError, because there is no reasonable whole number that the text "hello" represents. int(7.9) does not fail, but it truncates toward zero rather than rounding, producing 7, not 8; if you actually want standard rounding, the built-in round() function is the correct tool, and round(7.9) produces 8. Casting a string that is not a valid number, or casting None, will also raise errors, so explicit casts are a place in your code worth double-checking, especially around user input.

Casting to bool is a special case worth calling out on its own: bool(0), bool(0.0), bool(""), and bool([]) all produce False, while bool applied to anything else produces True, including bool(-1), which surprises some beginners who expect only 0 to be falsy and forget that negative numbers are still nonzero. Explicit casting, used deliberately at the exact point where a type genuinely needs to change, is what turns type conversion from something that happens to your code into something your code controls.

float() casting has its own quirk worth knowing: it accepts strings with a decimal point, so float("3.14") correctly produces 3.14, but it also accepts plain whole-number-looking strings, so float("7") produces 7.0, a float, not an int. Casting in the other direction, from a collection of bools to a count, is also a common trick built directly on the fact that bool is a subtype of int: int(True) produces 1, and sum([True, False, True, True]) produces 3 without needing an explicit cast at all, since sum() already treats each True as 1 internally, the same behavior noted back in the boolean type lesson.
